questions.stem: What proves the collected gas is oxygen?

options.text: A glowing splint relights when placed in the sample
options.explanation: Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.

options.text: The gas dissolves in the water
options.explanation: Oxygen collection is visible as bubbles.

options.text: The gas smells fresh
options.explanation: Smell identifies nothing here.

options.text: The water turns clear
options.explanation: No colour change occurs.

questions.stem: Where do the oxygen bubbles originate?

options.text: From the beaker's surface
options.explanation: Surface air is not the source.

options.text: From the cut end of the submerged pondweed stem
options.explanation: Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.

options.text: From the funnel's rim
options.explanation: The funnel only channels gas.

options.text: From the boiling tube's water
options.explanation: The tube collects, it does not generate.

questions.stem: How can the same setup measure the rate of photosynthesis?

options.text: By timing the splint test
options.explanation: The splint test identifies gas, not rate.

options.text: By measuring water temperature
options.explanation: Temperature is not varied or measured here.

options.text: By counting bubbles, or the collected volume, over a fixed time
options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.

options.text: By weighing the plant hourly
options.explanation: Mass change is not the read-out.

questions.stem: Why must the plant be submerged under the funnel?

options.text: To keep the plant from drying
options.explanation: Submersion is the natural state of pondweed.

options.text: To cool the plant
options.explanation: Cooling is not the funnel's function.

options.text: To add carbon dioxide to the water
options.explanation: The setup does not supply gas.

options.text: So released oxygen bubbles are channelled into the boiling tube for collection
options.explanation: Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.

questions.stem: Which apparatus item is reserved for the oxygen test itself?

options.text: The splint, lit and used to relight in the gas
options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.

options.text: The cork borer
options.explanation: No cork borer appears in this setup.

options.text: The boiling tube holder
options.explanation: Holding hardware is not the test.

options.text: The ethanol
options.explanation: Ethanol belongs to the starch test.

questions.stem: Name the test used to identify oxygen gas.
questions.modelAnswer: The glowing splint test, which relights in the presence of oxygen.

questions.stem: State what is collected in the inverted boiling tube.
questions.modelAnswer: Oxygen gas released by the photosynthesising pondweed collects there, displacing water.

questions.stem: Explain why bubble count rises when the lamp is moved closer.
questions.modelAnswer: Because closer light raises the intensity reaching the plant, photosynthesis speeds up, and oxygen is released faster; the bubble stream thins out again only when another factor becomes limiting.

questions.stem: A student's pondweed stops bubbling after an hour under bright light. Suggest the likely limiting factor.
questions.modelAnswer: The most likely limiting factor is dissolved carbon dioxide, which the plant has exhausted from the water; light remains bright and temperature steady, so the scarcest resource — carbon dioxide — now caps the rate and the bubbling stops.

questions.stem: Why is starch, not glucose, tested for in the leaf?

options.text: Starch dissolves faster for testing
options.explanation: Starch is actually insoluble and stored.

options.text: Glucose is used up or transported quickly, while starch persists where it was made
options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.

options.text: Glucose is invisible to iodine only
options.explanation: The persistence of starch is the stated reason.

options.text: Glucose is toxic to the leaf
options.explanation: Glucose is the plant's own product.

questions.stem: What is the purpose of de-starching the plant in a dark cupboard?

options.text: To make iodine react faster
options.explanation: De-starching affects the leaf, not the reagent.

options.text: To remove the chlorophyll early
options.explanation: Chlorophyll removal happens in ethanol later.

options.text: So any starch already present is used up and cannot confuse the result
options.explanation: Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.

options.text: To kill the leaf's cells
options.explanation: The leaf stays alive.

questions.stem: Why is ethanol heated in a water bath rather than over a flame?

options.text: Water bath heats ethanol faster
options.explanation: Safety, not speed, is the reason.

options.text: Ethanol dissolves the boiling tube
options.explanation: Glass is unaffected.

options.text: Iodine decomposes over flames
options.explanation: Iodine is added later, at room temperature.

options.text: Ethanol catches fire easily, so it stays far from naked flames
options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.

questions.stem: What result does the foil-covered area of the leaf show after iodine?

options.text: It remains orange-brown, showing no starch was made there
options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.

options.text: It turns blue-black like the rest
options.explanation: Only illuminated areas store starch.

options.text: It turns the leaf white
options.explanation: Bleaching happened earlier, for both areas.

options.text: It dissolves the leaf tissue
options.explanation: The leaf stays intact for staining.

questions.stem: Why must chlorophyll be removed before staining?

options.text: Because ethanol needs a second use
options.explanation: The ethanol step is single-purpose.

options.text: So the iodine's colour change can be seen clearly against the pale leaf
options.explanation: Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.

options.text: Because chlorophyll destroys iodine
options.explanation: No such reaction is cited.

options.text: Because green leaves cannot absorb iodine
options.explanation: Absorption is fine; visibility is the issue.

questions.stem: State the colour iodine shows in the presence of starch.
questions.modelAnswer: Iodine turns the leaf blue-black where starch is present.

questions.stem: Name the solvent used to remove chlorophyll from the leaf.
questions.modelAnswer: Hot ethanol removes the green chlorophyll from the leaf.

questions.stem: Explain why the foil experiment proves light is necessary for starch production.
questions.modelAnswer: Because the same leaf, treated identically, stains blue-black only where light reached it and stays orange-brown under the foil; the single controlled difference is illumination, so light must be required for the photosynthesis that laid down the starch.

questions.stem: A student forgets the de-starching step. Predict the result and the conclusion it threatens.
questions.modelAnswer: Old starch from before the experiment may still stain blue-black even under the foil, making both areas blue-black; the student could wrongly conclude that light is unnecessary, when in fact residual starch blurred the test.

questions.stem: What does potassium hydroxide do inside the conical flask?

options.text: It supplies water to the leaf
options.explanation: The leaf is attached to the plant, not the flask liquid.

options.text: It stains the leaf for starch
options.explanation: Staining is iodine's job later.

options.text: It absorbs carbon dioxide from the surrounding air
options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.

options.text: It releases carbon dioxide
options.explanation: It removes the gas, which is the point.

questions.stem: Why is a flask without potassium hydroxide included?

options.text: To double the starch yield
options.explanation: Yield is not the design's purpose.

options.text: To keep the plant moist
options.explanation: Moisture comes from the plant itself.

options.text: To absorb oxygen instead
options.explanation: The chemical's role is carbon dioxide removal in the treated flask only.

options.text: As a control, to show the leaf photosynthesises when carbon dioxide is available
options.explanation: Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.

questions.stem: What result does the potassium hydroxide leaf give after iodine?

options.text: It remains orange-brown, showing no starch was produced
options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.

options.text: It turns blue-black like the control
options.explanation: Without carbon dioxide no starch was made.

options.text: It turns the solution green
options.explanation: The leaf does not colour the flask.

options.text: It shows the five-step colour change
options.explanation: That diagram belongs to the starch-test method.

questions.stem: Which steps prepare each leaf before the light exposure?

options.text: Adding iodine before the light
options.explanation: Iodine is the final test, after the exposure.

options.text: De-starching the whole plant for a day in darkness
options.explanation: Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.

options.text: Boiling the leaves immediately
options.explanation: Boiling happens only at the starch-test stage.

options.text: Covering one leaf with foil
options.explanation: Foil belongs to the light experiment.

questions.stem: What conclusion does the paired-flask experiment support?

options.text: Potassium hydroxide is a plant nutrient
options.explanation: It is an absorbent chemical, not a nutrient.

options.text: Starch can be made without photosynthesis
options.explanation: The treated leaf's failure shows the opposite.

options.text: Carbon dioxide is necessary for photosynthesis and starch production
options.explanation: Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.

options.text: Light is unnecessary when flasks are used
options.explanation: Light was provided to both leaves.

questions.stem: State the role of the control flask in this experiment.
questions.modelAnswer: The control flask holds no potassium hydroxide, so its leaf photosynthesises normally for comparison.

questions.stem: Name the chemical that absorbs carbon dioxide in this setup.
questions.modelAnswer: Potassium hydroxide solution absorbs the carbon dioxide inside the flask.

questions.stem: Explain why both leaves must come from the same de-starched plant.
questions.modelAnswer: Because starting starch levels and plant condition must match; a leaf from another plant, or one still holding starch, would confound the iodine result and break the one-variable design that makes the conclusion trustworthy.

questions.stem: The treated leaf surprisingly stains blue-black. Evaluate the investigation.
questions.modelAnswer: A blue-black treated leaf suggests the carbon dioxide absorption failed — perhaps the flask leaked or the potassium hydroxide was exhausted — so the investigation should be repeated with a sealed flask and fresh chemical before any conclusion is drawn.
